lead: Mass transfer is the movement of one component through a mixture because that component is more concentrated in one place than in another. Refining crude oil, drying a shirt on a balcony, scrubbing CO2 out of flue gas, and your blood picking up oxygen all work the same way: a concentration difference pushes a species from a rich region to a lean one. Almost every separation that works by moving a component between phases is a named way of arranging that push. Mechanical separations such as filtration and centrifugation are a different family and are not part of this subject. This chapter defines the subject, sorts the operations into families, and fixes the vocabulary of concentration that every later formula uses.
prereq: You need mole and mass balances, the ideal gas law, and the idea of a phase from the thermodynamics course; no earlier chapter of this unit is assumed.

sections.h3: Mass transfer: one component moving because it is unevenly spread

blocks.text: Mass transfer is the movement of a component inside a mixture, or from one phase to another, driven by a difference in concentration. Concentration here means how much of that component sits in a given volume or in a given number of moles. The component moves from where it is rich to where it is lean. No pump, no stirrer and no heat are needed for the movement itself.

Compare the three transport subjects. Heat transfer moves energy because of a temperature difference. Fluid flow moves the whole mixture together because of a pressure difference. Mass transfer moves one species relative to the others because of a concentration difference. A river carrying salt to the sea moves water and salt together — that is fluid flow. Salt slowly spreading from a salty patch into a fresh patch of the same river is mass transfer.

The subject exists because almost every separation in a chemical plant is built on this one movement. You contact two phases, arrange that one phase prefers the wanted component, and diffusion carries it across. Two examples: CO2 washed out of flue gas by an amine solution, and sugar leached from chopped cane by hot water.

sections.h3: Four families, sorted by how the second phase is made

blocks.text: A single phase cannot be separated by mass transfer alone. Separation needs a second phase — immiscible, or only partly miscible, with the first — that holds the wanted component more strongly or more weakly. The four families below differ only in how that second phase is produced. Knowing the family tells you which unit of this subject you are reading.

items: Phase creation — heat or work makes a new phase out of the feed. Distillation, where heat raises a vapour; evaporation, where solvent is boiled off; crystallization, where cooling or concentrating makes solid appear. See Unit 4 and Unit 6.

Phase addition — a foreign liquid or gas is added and it dissolves the wanted component. Absorption (gas into liquid), extraction (solute from one liquid into another), leaching (solute from a solid into a liquid). See Unit 3 and Unit 5.
Barrier — a membrane lets one species through faster than another. Reverse osmosis passes water and holds salt back; dialysis passes small molecules and holds large ones. See Unit 6.
Solid agent — a solid surface or resin takes up the solute. Adsorption on activated carbon, ion exchange on a resin. See Unit 6.

blocks.text: Most books place drying with hot gas under phase creation, since heat makes the vapour; a few treat the hot gas as an added phase and put it under phase addition. Drying is never a solid-agent operation in the adsorption sense, because the solid gives up water rather than taking up solute. For any operation named in an exam, state which component moves and which phase is new.

sections.h3: Phases in contact, contactors, and the four numbers called concentration

blocks.text: The same operations are also sorted by the phases that touch. Gas-liquid: absorption, distillation. Liquid-liquid: extraction. Gas-solid: adsorption, drying. Liquid-solid: leaching, ion exchange, crystallization. Each pair brings its own equipment, its own equilibrium relation and its own mass transfer coefficient, which is why the later units are organised this way.

A third sorting is by contactor. A stage-wise contactor mixes the two phases, lets them approach equilibrium, then separates them; a tray column is a stack of such stages. A differential contactor keeps the phases in touch continuously along a path, so composition changes smoothly from end to end; a packed tower, a falling film and a spray are examples. Batch and continuous cut across both. Contactor behaviour is developed in Unit 2.
Four different numbers are all called concentration. Learn them now, because every flux formula later needs the right one.

blocks.where: c is the total molar concentration of an ideal gas, mol/m³; P is the absolute pressure, Pa; T is the absolute temperature, K; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is the gas constant. For a liquid the molar density is c = ρ/M, with ρ in kg/m³ and M in kg/mol. One relation ties the mass and mole worlds together: ρ<sub>A</sub> = c<sub>A</sub> M<sub>A</sub>, with ρ<sub>A</sub> in kg/m³, c<sub>A</sub> in mol/m³ and M<sub>A</sub> in kg/mol (divide a molar mass given in g/mol by 1000 first).

examples.question: A flue gas at 1 atm and 300 K contains 22 mol% CO2 and 78 mol% air. Take M(air) = 29 g/mol, M(CO2) = 44 g/mol, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and 1 atm = 101325 Pa. Find (a) the mean molar mass, (b) the mass fraction of CO2, (c) the total molar concentration, (d) the mass concentration of CO2 in kg/m³.
steps: Mass fraction: w(CO2) = y(CO2)·M(CO2) / M̄ = 9.68 / 32.3 = 0.300, that is 30.0 % by mass.
Total molar concentration from the ideal gas law: c = P / (R T) = 101325 / (8.314 × 300) = 101325 / 2494.2 = 40.6 mol/m³.
CO2 molar concentration: c(CO2) = y(CO2)·c = 0.22 × 40.6 = 8.93 mol/m³.
CO2 mass concentration: ρ(CO2) = c(CO2)·M(CO2) = 8.93 × 0.044 kg/mol = 0.393 kg/m³.
examples.answer: The gas has a mean molar mass of 32.3 g/mol, a CO2 mass fraction of 0.300, a total concentration of 40.6 mol/m³ and a CO2 mass concentration of 0.393 kg/m³.

traps: Writing 'concentration' without saying which one. Mole fraction and mass fraction are dimensionless and are not concentrations; a flux needs mol/m³ or kg/m³. Converting a molar concentration to a mass concentration multiplies by the molar mass in kg/mol. Always write the symbol and the unit.
Using c = P/RT for a liquid. That formula holds for an ideal gas only. For a liquid use the molar density c = ρ/M, with ρ in kg/m³ and M in kg/mol.

Swapping y and x. By long convention y is the mole fraction in the vapour or gas and x is the mole fraction in the liquid. An answer that writes x for a gas stream loses marks even when the number is right.
Thinking mass transfer needs bulk flow. Diffusion carries a species through a completely still mixture; diffusion and bulk flow are separated properly in 1.2.

Classifying by equipment instead of by mechanism. A packed tower is not a separation; it is a contactor that can carry out absorption, stripping or distillation, and the examiner often asks you to say which.

quiz.q: Define mass transfer and state its driving force.
quiz.a: Mass transfer is the movement of a component within a mixture, or from one phase to another, because that component is more concentrated in one place than another. The driving force is the concentration difference, or more strictly a difference in chemical potential.

quiz.q: Name the four families of mass transfer operations, sorted by how the second phase is made, with one example each.
quiz.a: Phase creation (distillation), phase addition (absorption), barrier (reverse osmosis), solid agent (adsorption).

quiz.q: Why does distillation belong to phase creation and absorption to phase addition?
quiz.a: In distillation the second phase is made out of the feed itself: heat turns part of the liquid into vapour. In absorption the second phase is brought in from outside as a foreign liquid that dissolves the solute; the feed does not create it.

quiz.q: Give one clear difference between a stage-wise and a differential contactor.
quiz.a: In a stage-wise contactor the phases are mixed, brought near equilibrium and then separated, so composition changes in steps (a tray column). In a differential contactor the phases touch continuously along a path, so composition changes smoothly from one end to the other (a packed tower or a falling film).

quiz.q: A gas at 2 atm and 350 K contains 15 mol% CO2. Take R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and 1 atm = 101325 Pa. Find the total molar concentration and the CO2 molar concentration.
A liquid of density 900 kg/m³ has molar mass 60 g/mol. Find its molar density in mol/m³.
quiz.a: c = ρ/M = 900/0.060 = 15000 mol/m³, that is 15.0 kmol/m³.

quiz.q: A plant must remove CO2 from flue gas. Explain why a second phase cannot be avoided, and place the chosen operation on the classification tree.
quiz.a: CO2 in one gas phase cannot be separated from the other gases by mass transfer alone; a second phase must take CO2 up more strongly than the flue gas does. An amine solution added as a liquid does this, so the operation is absorption, which sits under phase addition; the phases in contact are gas-liquid and the usual contactor is a packed tower.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most new work sits in the barrier family: membrane gas separation for CO2 capture, forward osmosis for desalination, and pervaporation for solvent recovery. Process intensification tries to merge two families into one vessel, for example a membrane reactor or a reactive distillation column where reaction and separation happen together. Search 'membrane gas separation' and 'process intensification' to go further.
